title: Global Frost Events Benchmark Dataset
text:
This repository contains a curated collection of documented frost events across the globe.
The primary purpose of this dataset is to support the development, evaluation, and validation of frost detection algorithms, particularly those based on climate reanalysis data (e.g. ERA5) and crop models.
This dataset is not intended to be exhaustive. Instead, it provides a set of high-confidence, representative frost events across different regions, climates, and cropping systems.

title: Global Frost Events Benchmark Dataset
text:
Motivation
Frost remains a major constraint to agricultural production worldwide.
However, there is currently no standardised global dataset of frost events available for:

validating frost detection methods
comparing modelling approaches
benchmarking climate-based risk metrics

This repository aims to fill that gap by providing a transparent, reproducible benchmark dataset.

title: Spring Frost Impacts in Australia
text: Spring frost is a major constraint on agricultural production in southern Australia, typically occurring during September to October when crops are at sensitive reproductive stages. These events are often radiative in nature, associated with clear skies, low wind, and dry conditions, and can cause widespread yield losses across broadacre cropping systems.

title: Spring Frost Impacts in Australia
text:
Major impact regions

Western Australian Wheatbelt
A large and highly productive grain-growing region. Frost occurs frequently during flowering and grain-filling stages, leading to significant yield reductions in wheat, barley, and canola, particularly in low-lying landscape positions.


South Australia (Eyre Peninsula, Mid North)
A key frost-prone region with recurring spring frost events. Crops are often affected during flowering, with severe cases resulting in widespread damage, haying-off, or crop abandonment.


South-eastern Australia (Victoria, southern New South Wales)
Includes major cropping zones in Victoria and NSW. Frost events can impact large areas simultaneously, with damage varying depending on sowing time, crop development stage, and local topography.

title: Spring Frost Impacts in Australia
text:
Impact characteristics
Spring frost impacts in Australia are characterised by:

High phenological sensitivity: crops are most vulnerable during flowering and early grain development

Radiative frost dominance: clear, calm nights drive strong surface cooling

Topographic effects: cold air drainage leads to severe damage in low-lying areas

Repeated events: multiple frost nights within a short period increase cumulative damage

title: Spring Frost Impacts in Australia
text:
Summary
Spring frost is a widespread and recurrent hazard across southern Australia’s grain-producing regions. Its impacts are most severe when frost coincides with flowering, resulting in substantial yield and quality losses across wheat, barley, and canola systems. These conditions make Australia a key benchmark region for evaluating frost detection and impact models in broadacre agricultural systems.

title: Late Spring Frost Impacts in China
text: Late spring frost (“倒春寒” or “晚霜冻”) is a major agricultural hazard in China, occurring after crop re-growth and coinciding with highly sensitive developmental stages. These events are typically short in duration but can cause disproportionate reductions in yield and quality across both grain and horticultural systems.

title: Late Spring Frost Impacts in China
text: Late spring frost (“倒春寒” or “晚霜冻”) is a major agricultural hazard in China, occurring after crop re-growth and coinciding with highly sensitive developmental stages. These events are typically short in duration but can cause disproportionate reductions in yield and quality across both grain and horticultural systems.

title: Late Spring Frost Impacts in China
text:
Major impact regions

Loess Plateau (Shaanxi, Gansu)
A key fruit-producing region, particularly for apple. Frost during the flowering period frequently causes severe damage to blossoms, leading to large yield losses and strong interannual variability in production.


North China Plain (Hebei, Henan, Shandong)
China’s core winter wheat belt. Late frost events during jointing or heading stages reduce grain number and weight, with impacts occurring at regional scale due to the extensive cropping area.


Northern orchard regions (Bohai Rim)
Includes Hebei, Shandong, and Liaoning. Fruit trees such as apple, pear, and peach are highly vulnerable during bloom, with frost leading to failure of fruit set and significant economic loss.


Northeast China (Heilongjiang, Jilin)
An important maize and soybean region. Occasional late spring frost affects early growth stages, damaging seedlings and sometimes requiring replanting.


Southwest plateau (Yunnan, Guizhou)
Complex terrain creates localised frost-prone environments. Crops such as potato and tobacco are affected, with strong spatial variability driven by elevation and cold-air pooling.

title: Late Spring Frost Impacts in China
text:
Impact characteristics
Late spring frost impacts in China are characterised by:

High phenological sensitivity: damage occurs during flowering or early reproductive stages

Short duration but high intensity: often 1–3 nights below critical thresholds

Strong regional contrasts: from broadacre impacts in northern plains to localised frost pockets in complex terrain

Significant economic effects: particularly for high-value fruit systems

title: Late Spring Frost Impacts in China
text:
Summary
Late spring frost represents a critical constraint on agricultural production in China, with impacts concentrated in the Loess Plateau fruit systems, the North China Plain wheat belt, and orchard regions in northern China, alongside additional risks in the northeast and southwest. These events provide valuable benchmark cases for evaluating frost detection and impact models across diverse agro-climatic conditions.

title: South Australia Spring Frosts (2024)
text:
Meteorological context
The frost events developed during a very dry growing season, with many regions experiencing well below average rainfall. Multiple frost events occurred over a short period, including at least five days below 0°C in mid-September, with minimum temperatures reported as low as −6.5°C.
The extended duration and frequency of these events contributed to significant agricultural impact.

title: South Australia Spring Frosts (2024)
text:
Spatial definition
This event is defined over major cropping regions of South Australia, particularly the Eyre Peninsula and Mid North, where the most severe impacts were reported.
A bounding box is used to represent the affected region for analysis with gridded datasets such as ERA5.

title: South Australia Spring Frosts (2024)
text:
Impact
The frost events affected a wide range of crops, including wheat, lentils, barley, and canola. Many crops were at flowering or early grain development stages when frost occurred, increasing sensitivity.
Reports indicate substantial yield losses, with some regions experiencing severe damage requiring crops to be cut for hay or abandoned.

title: Global Frost Events Dataset: Data Collection Protocol
text:
This protocol defines the principles and procedures for identifying, collecting, and structuring frost events in the Global Frost Events dataset.
The dataset aims to compile a curated set of source-confirmed frost events impacting agriculture, designed for: - validation of frost detection algorithms - comparative analysis across regions and crops - reproducible research

title: Global Frost Events Dataset: Data Collection Protocol
text:
This protocol defines the principles and procedures for identifying, collecting, and structuring frost events in the Global Frost Events dataset.
The dataset aims to compile a curated set of source-confirmed frost events impacting agriculture, designed for: - validation of frost detection algorithms - comparative analysis across regions and crops - reproducible research

title: Global Frost Events Dataset: Data Collection Protocol
text:
Core principles

Event-based approach
Each dataset entry represents a real-world frost event, defined by: - documented occurrence - identifiable time window - confirmed agricultural impact
Events are not based on climatology or model output, but on explicit evidence from sources.


Evidence-driven geometry
Spatial information must be derived from source-confirmed observations, not inferred regions.
Each event contains:

geometry: a representative reference location
observations: a collection of source-backed spatial features

This ensures a clear distinction between: - observed locations (evidence) - derived geometries (used for analysis)


Separation of data and interpretation

meta.json stores structured, source-backed data
event.qmd provides narrative interpretation and context

No interpretation should be embedded in structured fields unless explicitly supported by sources.

title: Global Frost Events Dataset: Data Collection Protocol
text:
Event identification workflow

Step 1: Identify candidate events
Events should be identified from: - peer-reviewed publications - government or institutional reports - industry reports - credible news sources
Priority is given to: - well-documented events - events with clear agricultural impacts - events with identifiable timing and location


Step 2: Confirm event validity
An event is included only if: - frost occurrence is explicitly reported - agricultural impact is described or implied
